title: Strong Navratri Opening Lifts Diwali Hopes as Online Shoppers Keep Baskets Small
excerpt: Showroom demand hit a five-year high in the season's first phase, but festive online sales trail last year by up to 10% — while quick commerce climbs to a 16% share as mithai and gifts go last-minute.
body:
• India's festive season has opened strongly in stores: demand in the season's first phase hit a five-year high across cars, appliances, apparel and footwear, manufacturers told PTI.
  • Online tells a different story — festive e-commerce sales are trailing last year by up to 10%, with shoppers choosing smaller baskets, according to Datum Intelligence data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine.
  • Quick commerce is the season's structural winner: its share of festive sales is expected to reach 16%, up from 12% last year, as mithai, gifts and groceries are ordered closer to the festival.
  • The calendar is compressed: Navratri began October 11, Dussehra falls on October 20, Dhanteras on November 6 and Diwali on November 8 — most festive spending lands in the next four weeks.

India's festive season has opened with a split personality. In showrooms and high-street stores, Navratri demand has run ahead of expectations, extending a first phase of the season — Onam, Rakshabandhan and Ganesh Chaturthi — that manufacturers describe as the strongest in five years. Online, the same season is trailing last year, as shoppers buy more often but spend less each time.

The in-store surge

The opening phase delivered broad-based growth despite repeated price increases. Volume sales of refrigerators, air-conditioners and washing machines rose 12–15% year on year, while value sales grew faster, 18–23%, helped by higher prices. Automakers set the pace: Maruti Suzuki's retail sales during Onam jumped 61% year on year, Hyundai nearly doubled its sales and accelerated plans for a third shift at its Talegaon plant, and car dealers reported around 20% growth overall. Appliance makers expect the momentum to carry through Diwali — Haier India's chief executive projected industry growth of 10–15%, with premium products, replacement buying and easy finance doing the work.

The online caution

Against that, data from Datum Intelligence, reported by The Hindu BusinessLine, shows festive online sales trailing last year by up to 10% in the opening stretch, with smaller basket sizes and little excitement in smartphones — historically the category that powers festive e-commerce. Datum expects the first week to account for 46% of the season's online sales, down from 48% in 2025, which pushes a larger share of spending into the run-up to Diwali on November 8.

"Frankly, smartphone apart from the price, there's no buzz around the models also."

— Satish Meena, Datum Intelligence, on festive demand

Where food fits: smaller baskets, faster delivery

For festive food, the online shift cuts the other way. Quick commerce — the 10-minute delivery platforms — is expected to take 16% of festive sales this year, up from 12%, as households order mithai, dry fruits, gifting and puja supplies in smaller, more frequent baskets timed to each festival day rather than in one large shop. That is the pattern behind the "smaller baskets" concern: for marketplaces it dilutes the headline sale events; for neighbourhood sweet shops and quick-commerce dark stores it spreads demand across the whole season. Fashion, beauty and home categories are also expected to contribute a rising share as the season progresses.

Jaipur's opening day, in numbers

The Times of India's Jaipur reporting puts local scale on the national picture. Trade bodies estimate festive business of nearly Rs 50,000 crore across Rajasthan between Navratri and Diwali, including about Rs 10,000 crore in Jaipur alone, where strong first-day footfall in markets such as the Walled City lifted trader hopes. Automobile dealers reported demand up at least 30%, and the Jaipur Electronic Trade Association said first-day response beat expectations across televisions, refrigerators, washing machines and kitchen appliances, with sales expected to at least match last year. The concerns in the headline are specific: a deficient monsoon squeezing rural incomes, weak equity markets, inflation, and high gold and silver prices pushing younger jewellery buyers from 22-carat toward 18-carat and even 14-carat pieces. Shoppers, traders said, are spending — but selectively, protecting traditional and essential purchases first. The Federation of Rajasthan Trade and Industry called the wider economy "a mixed bag."

What to watch before Diwali

The calendar gives retailers four working weeks: Navratri began on October 11, Dussehra falls on October 20, and Dhanteras (November 6) and Diwali (November 8) close the season. Manufacturers are betting that showroom momentum outweighs online softness; the platforms are betting the spending simply arrives later this year. For diaspora readers sending gifts home, the practical read is that delivery slots and festive inventories will tighten sharply in the final week before November 8 — the week Datum's numbers say a growing share of India now leaves its festive buying to.
